# Teaching notes: from bacterial classes to trait logic

::: {.callout-warning}
## For teaching staff · draft for discussion
This page is not part of the student text. It maps the current MD1140 microbiology sessions onto the
approach used in this draft, as a starting point for discussion.
:::

## The proposal in brief {#sec-tn-brief}

**Keep the sessions organised by bacterial class, but change what holds each one together.** At
present a class session tends to run *organism → infections → diagnosis → antibiotics*, repeated for
each organism. Students meet many organism–disease–drug combinations with no shared structure, so
they try to memorise them.

The alternative keeps the same classes and asks the same six questions of each:

1. What is it built from?
2. How does it get energy, and what does it need to grow?
3. How does it copy itself and change?
4. Where does it live, and how does it spread?
5. How does damage happen, and how much is microbe versus host?
6. What does it have that my cells lack?

Each class session then teaches **why the class behaves as it does**. The specific infections,
diagnostic pathways and drug choices move to the organ-system blocks and pharmacology, where students
attach them to a structure they already have.

**Why this is worth trying.** No trial has compared the two approaches in medical students, so the
case rests on expert consensus and learning science from other fields:

- The 2026 AMSMIC core objectives make the foundational layer pathogen-free and call for moving beyond
  the "bug parade" [@bauler2026objectives].
- Students taught causal mechanisms kept more after a week than students taught feature lists (62%
  versus 51%), in non-infectious conditions.
- Actively comparing two similar cases teaches more than studying each alone [@alfieri2013contrasting].
- Retrieval practice with feedback, spaced over weeks, is one of the best-supported study methods.

The full evidence review is in the project's research report.

## Session crosswalk {#sec-tn-crosswalk}

For each session: what stays as foundation content, what can move later, and where the draft
already shows it. Chapter names in italics are chapters of this book.

::: {.column-page}

| Session | Keep at foundation level | Move to organ-system blocks | Move to pharmacology | In this draft |
|------------------|------------------------------------|------------------|------------|----------------|
| Introduction to microbiology and infectious diseases | Scale; prokaryote versus eukaryote; most microbes are harmless; the six questions | — | — | *The microbial world*; *How bacteria are built* |
| How microbes cause disease | Colonisation versus disease; damage from microbe versus host; toxins, invasion, survival in cells; host factors | Named diseases | — | *Microbes and their hosts* (outline) |
| Staphylococci and streptococci | Gram-positive cocci; clusters versus chains; catalase; why infections form pus; carriage | Skin, throat, heart and bone infections | Drug choice; MRSA | **Gram-positive cocci (full test chapter)** |
| Infections caused by Enterobacterales | Gram-negative facultative gut rods; LPS; harmless residents versus strains with extra genes | Gut, urinary and bloodstream infections | Resistant strains in detail | *Enterobacterales* (outline); map and pair in *A map of the bacteria* |
| Case studies (F2F) | Recast as mechanism or investigation cases rather than diagnose-and-treat | Clinical cases | — | Lab case in *How bacteria are built*; outbreak case in *Gram-positive cocci* |
| Epidemiology of infectious diseases | Reservoirs, routes, incubation, carriers, outbreaks, One Health | Syndrome-specific epidemiology | — | *Transmission, outbreaks and One Health* (outline) |
| Diagnostic bacteriology | What each method reads: stains read the envelope, culture reads growth needs, tests read metabolism, DNA tests bypass culture | Which test for which syndrome | — | Gram stain and oxygen tube in *How bacteria are built*; *Detecting and controlling microbes* (outline) |
| Fastidious Gram-negative infections | "Fastidious" as lost biosynthesis; why enriched media work | Respiratory and heart-valve infections | Drug choice | *Fastidious Gram-negatives and Gram-negative cocci* (outline) |
| Pseudomonads, vibrios and Burkholderia | Environmental Gram-negatives; metabolism predicts habitat; natural resistance; melioidosis and diabetes as a host-factor anchor | Hospital infections; cholera; melioidosis presentations | Anti-pseudomonal drugs | *Environmental Gram-negatives* (outline); pair in *A map of the bacteria* |
| Infections caused by Gram-negative cocci | Fragility explains close-contact spread; the capsule in the blood | Meningitis; gonorrhoea | Treatment and prophylaxis | *Fastidious Gram-negatives and Gram-negative cocci* (outline) |
| Anaerobic infections | Why oxygen harms anaerobes; oxygen-poor niches; abscess logic; sample handling | Abdominal, dental and other mixed infections | Drug choice | Oxygen sections and lab case in *How bacteria are built*; *Anaerobes* (outline) |
| Infections caused by Gram-positive bacilli | Spores; disease from a single toxin; *Listeria* growing in the cold and inside cells | Tetanus, botulism, diphtheria presentations | Drug choice | *Gram-positive rods* (outline) |
| Infections caused by spiral bacteria | Internal flagella and corkscrew motility; hard to see or grow, so detected indirectly; ticks and rats as reservoirs | Syphilis stages; leptospirosis; Lyme disease | Drug choice | *Spiral bacteria* (outline) |
| Atypical infections: *Chlamydia*, *Mycoplasma*, *Rickettsia* | Two reasons the toolkit fails: no wall, or only inside cells; what each predicts for staining, culture and drug targets | Atypical pneumonia; sexually transmitted chlamydia; rickettsial fevers | Drug choice | Worked example in *A map of the bacteria*; *Atypicals and mycobacteria* (outline) |
| Infection control practical and STD case management (F2F) | Sterilisation versus disinfection; why alcohol rub misses spores; transmission routes | Case management | — | *Detecting and controlling microbes* (outline); spores in *How bacteria are built* |
| Antibiotic resistance: threats and stewardship | Selection acts on existing variation; gene transfer; "the body becomes resistant" corrected; stewardship as a population idea | Resistance in specific infections | Drug classes and mechanisms | *How bacteria copy themselves and change* (outline); MRSA in *Gram-positive cocci* |

:::

## Before and after: the atypicals session {#sec-tn-before-after}

The same 60-minute self-directed session, in two shapes. The first column is a typical class-based
outline, not a transcript of any particular session.

| | Class-based outline | Trait-logic outline |
|---|---|---|
| Spine | Three organisms, each in turn | Two reasons the usual toolkit fails |
| Opening | Definitions and classification | Predict: "A bacterium has no wall. What will the Gram stain, culture and wall-targeting drugs do?" |
| Middle | For each organism: features, diseases, clinical picture, diagnosis, treatment | *Mycoplasma* profile, predicted slot by slot (about 15 min); *Mycoplasma* versus *Chlamydia* contrast and sort (10 min); *Rickettsia* as a second "inside cells" example, adding vectors (5 min) |
| Practice | End-of-session MCQs on facts | Mixed retrieval on the bacteria map: name the group from its traits (10 min) |
| Disease detail | Full, for each organism | A short "you will meet these again in the respiratory and genitourinary blocks" list |
| What students carry away | About 15 organism–disease–drug facts | Two ideas that predict those facts when they meet them later |

The trait-logic version is built in this draft: see **Worked example: why "atypical"?** in the
*A map of the bacteria* chapter.

## Depth and coverage: the group-chapter budget {#sec-tn-depth}

The *Gram-positive cocci* chapter is the test case for how deep a group chapter should go. It covers
the content of the "Staphylococci and streptococci" session within this budget:

| Element | Budget in the test chapter |
|---|---|
| Main organisms | 3 (*S. aureus*, *S. pyogenes*, *S. pneumoniae*), each with a full profile card |
| Supporting organisms | 4, one table row each: where it lives, the separating trait, why it matters |
| Diseases | Only as **patterns of harm**: mechanism, then one named example. No clinical features or diagnostic criteria |
| Lab tests | Only those that read a trait: catalase, coagulase, haemolysis, Lancefield group |
| Drugs | None by name. Resistance appears once, as a concept (MRSA as an altered drug target) |
| Activities | Sorting key, three profiles, two contrast pairs, quiz with mixed items, flashcards, one outbreak case |
| Length | About 2,500 words of prose, roughly one self-directed session |

**Questions for the meeting:** Is three main organisms right, or too few? Are any of the supporting
organisms important enough to be main? Is "one named example per mechanism" enough for MD1140, or does
the course need more disease names at this stage?

## What a session looks like in this format {#sec-tn-template}

Each class session in this draft uses the same parts, which makes sessions quicker to write and
easier for students to navigate:

- [ ] Open with one prediction that students can answer by reasoning from earlier material.
- [ ] Answer the six questions at foundation level only.
- [ ] One or two **contrast pairs**, chosen from the confusions students actually make.
- [ ] A **microbe profile** card for each example organism, with some slots left for students to predict.
- [ ] A refutation box wherever a common misconception exists.
- [ ] A short "later in the course" note naming what the organ-system blocks will add.
- [ ] Quiz items that ask *why*, with feedback that explains the mechanism.
- [ ] A few flashcards for spaced review.

## Questions for discussion {#sec-tn-questions}

1. **Scope.** Which disease, diagnosis and drug facts must stay in MD1140, and which can move to the
   organ-system blocks or pharmacology?
2. **Contrast pairs.** Which organisms do students most often confuse? Those pairs should drive the
   comparison activities.
3. **Session titles.** Should "Infections caused by Enterobacterales" become something like "How
   Enterobacterales live", to signal the change in emphasis?
4. **Assessment.** If teaching shifts to mechanisms, should MCQs shift to *why* questions too?
5. **Other organisms.** Viruses, fungi and parasites are only outlined here. Would you like to co-design
   those units?
6. **Evaluation.** Could one session be piloted next year, with a short concept check before and after?
   No data on Singapore medical students' microbiology misconceptions exist, so the results would also
   be publishable.
